hints: Notice the question tells you energy is released, so start by reminding yourself what exothermic really means for the surroundings.
Remember the golden rule: breaking bonds always takes energy in, while forming bonds always gives energy out.
For a net release of heat, compare the sizes of those two energy changes and decide which one must be larger.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the energy change**

Well done for spotting the key clue. 55 kJ per mol is released, so this neutralisation is exothermic.

$$\Delta H = -55 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Recall the bond energy rule**

Think of it simply like this. You must put energy in to pull atoms apart, but you get energy back when new bonds snap together.

Breaking bonds: endothermic, energy taken in.

Forming bonds: exothermic, energy given out.

**Compare breaking and forming**

Every chemical change involves both breaking and forming, never only one. The overall $\Delta H$ is the difference:
$$\Delta H = \text{energy in to break bonds} - \text{energy out to form bonds}$$
For $\Delta H$ to be negative, the energy given out in forming must be bigger than the energy taken in to break.

options.A: Incorrect. Bond breaking alone can never make a reaction exothermic because breaking bonds always absorbs energy. This reaction also involves both breaking (O-H) and forming (new O-H in water and ionic bonds).
options.B: Incorrect. It is true that bond forming releases energy, but it is wrong to say only bond forming happens. In neutralisation, $\text{O-H}$ bonds are broken first, then new bonds are formed to make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$.
options.C: Incorrect. This reverses the logic. Breaking bonds takes energy in, it does not give energy out. If more energy were given out in breaking than taken in to form, the reaction would be endothermic, not exothermic.
options.D: Correct. This is exactly the definition of exothermic. More energy is released when new bonds form (in water and sodium ethanoate) than is absorbed to break the old bonds in $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NaOH}$, giving a net release of 55 kJ mol-1.
